title: DI-Bench: Systematically Generating In-Domain Data Intelligence Benchmarks for Enterprise Agents
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 4 Sep 2026]
    Title:DI-Bench: Systematically Generating In-Domain Data Intelligence Benchmarks for Enterprise Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Evaluating enterprise agents on domain-specific benchmarks is critical, yet public benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can integrate business knowledge with analytical computation, and constructing such benchmarks manually is costly. We present DI-Bench, a pipeline for generating realistic benchmarks for data intelligence (DI), the practice of extracting insights from large volumes of enterprise data. To emulate realistic DI tasks that require both computation and knowledge retrieval, DI-Bench builds an artifact linkage graph over data tables, dimensions, metrics, and documents to form questions involving structured data and associated knowledge. Ground truth answers are derived via query execution, followed by LLM question generation and validation. Applied to two public datasets, the pipeline produces a 731-task benchmark covering knowledge retrieval, analytical computation, and rule-grounded reasoning. To show the discriminatory capability and difficulty of the benchmark, we evaluate four models, revealing a substantial finding: models achieve only 32% accuracy when doing computational tasks where retrieved business rules modify the computation.

report.summary: DI-Bench auto-generates enterprise data-intelligence benchmarks from linked tables, metrics, and documents, revealing models score only 32% when retrieved business rules alter computation.
report.background: Enterprise AI agents are increasingly expected to answer business questions by combining structured data analysis with unstructured policy and rule documents. Yet most public benchmarks evaluate text-to-SQL or retrieval-augmented QA in isolation, not the integrated data intelligence (DI) work real analysts do: querying tables, applying metric definitions, and respecting business rules found in documents. Manually building such benchmarks is expensive and slow, and they quickly become stale. Meanwhile, LLMs are being deployed for enterprise analytics, but without reliable domain-specific evaluation, organizations cannot tell whether an agent truly understands their data, metrics, and governance constraints. DI-Bench addresses this gap with an automated generation pipeline.
key_points: DI-Bench builds an artifact linkage graph connecting data tables, dimensions, metrics, and documents. This graph lets the generator create questions that require both analytical computation over structured data and retrieval of associated business knowledge, emulating real enterprise data-intelligence tasks rather than isolated SQL or QA problems.

The pipeline derives ground-truth answers by executing queries against the linked artifacts, then uses an LLM to generate natural-language questions and validate them. Applied to two public datasets, it produced a 731-task benchmark spanning knowledge retrieval, analytical computation, and rule-grounded reasoning.

To test discrimination, the authors evaluated four models. The headline result: models achieved only 32% accuracy on computational tasks where retrieved business rules modify the computation. This shows current agents struggle when they must integrate textual policy with numeric analysis, a core enterprise requirement.

The benchmark is notable for targeting rule-grounded reasoning, not just formulaic aggregation. Questions often require finding a document clause, interpreting it, and adjusting a calculation accordingly. This mirrors real workflows such as revenue recognition, compliance checks, or pricing exceptions, where ignoring context leads to wrong answers.
report.impact: DI-Bench signals that enterprise AI evaluation is moving from simple text-to-SQL toward integrated knowledge-and-computation reasoning. For the AI industry, it provides a scalable, low-cost way to create in-domain benchmarks, potentially shifting how vendors prove agent reliability. Developers building analytics agents will need architectures that retrieve rules, bind them to schema elements, and apply them during query planning or post-processing; naive RAG plus SQL will not suffice. For regular users, the 32% score is a warning: do not trust agent-generated business insights without verification, especially when policies or definitions matter. The benchmark also creates pressure for more transparent, auditable agents. Over time, such benchmarks could become standard procurement criteria for enterprise AI, rewarding systems that handle governed data intelligence rather than generic question answering.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the DI-Bench pipeline and dataset if released on Hugging Face or GitHub. Related evaluation resources include BIRD and Spider 2.0 for text-to-SQL, Ragas and DeepEval for retrieval-augmented generation metrics, and LangSmith or OpenAI Evals for agent tracing. For building rule-aware agents, explore LangChain, LlamaIndex, and DSPy for retrieval plus computation orchestration. Semantic layers like Cube or dbt can help encode business metrics and rules that DI-Bench-style tasks require.
